requirements.evidence: Migrations match the spec exactly: 'entities_slug_unique', softDeletes, a stored generated column `owner_seq` ->storedAs("case when role = 'owner' then 1 else null end") and the unique indexes 'entity_memberships_one_owner' and 'entity_memberships_entity_user_unique' (create_entity_memberships_table.php:16-25). The models, enum (`manageable()`), User relations and `membershipFor`, the factory states and both policies follow the contract. EntityPickController authorizes `view`, puts `current_entity_id` in the session, writes to Log::channel('audit') and redirects. Every Livewire page authorizes in mount() and holds a #[Locked] Entity. The dashboard shows the settings link and the owner notice only under @can('manageSettings'). Members validates 'required|email|exists:users,email', returns a duplicate as an error on email (AddMember.php:24-26), restricts roles with Rule::enum(...)->only(manageable()), and refuses to remove the owner or the last manager. Settings: the slug is unique except for itself (Rule::unique()->ignore), delete clears the session, transfer handles the admin-only target, demotes the owner first and returns 403 when the owner row is gone (TransferOwnership.php:26-34). The routes, lang keys in both locales and the docs update are all present.

conventions.evidence: Domain writes go through new app/Actions/* classes (AddMember, AssignRole, RemoveMember, UpdateEntity, DeleteEntity, TransferOwnership), and each one authorizes inside with Gate::forUser($actor)->authorize. Livewire uses #[Validate] and rules() together with $this->validate(). Mass assignment is controlled with #[Fillable]. Migrations have generated-style timestamps and a reversible down(). The views use the existing <x-form-field>/<x-button> components and Bulma classes. CHANGELOG, docs/database-schema.md and docs/business-rules.md are updated. One deviation: Settings::$targetMembershipId is a public property with no #[Validate] (Settings.php:31), which goes against policy rule 1, although the docblock explains why and the action checks the value.

security.evidence: Every public action is authorized on the server, through $this->authorize in the component or Gate inside the action. Action parameters are resolved only inside the bound entity: Members::membership() uses filter_var plus $this->entity->memberships()->find($id) and aborts with 403. The transfer target is checked with $entity->memberships()->admin()->whereKey($targetId)->lockForUpdate(). Entity is #[Locked] on all three components. Writes run in transactions with row locks. Output is escaped with {{ }} everywhere, and I found no {!! !!}. The database enforces the one-owner rule.

tests.evidence: There are six test files covering the models and schema (index names, generated column, duplicate owner rejected), the policies (each ability and role, plus outsiders), pick (session, audit log mock, 403 with the session left untouched, guest/unverified, 404 for deleted), the dashboard (settings URL hidden for admin/employee, both translations, 403 even when the session points elsewhere), members, and settings. Members tests cover adding, validation failures, duplicates, employee 403, 'owner'/'superuser' role errors, forged ids (another entity's membership, 999999, an array), last manager and self-leave. Settings tests cover validation datasets, lost-ownership races, delete with and without the current session entity, transfer refusals (employee, self, foreign admin, null, garbage, array), the vanished owner and locked-entity tamper tests.

simplicity.evidence: The code is direct, and policies reuse User::membershipFor(). The one-owner rule is enforced in the database instead of through extra application code. Small extras: separate filter_var id parsing in Members::membership() and in TransferOwnership, and audit log lines in every action, which the task does not require outside pick.

readability.evidence: Methods are small, names are clear, and PHPDoc explains the non-obvious decisions ('Demote first: the unique owner index never sees two owners.', 'Resolve the membership inside this entity; anything else is a forged id.'). The style matches the sibling Laravel/Livewire code, and there is no dead code or debug output.

scope.evidence: Every file serves the task. Onboarding, the switcher, the session-guard middleware, the locale middleware and navbar changes were not touched. The routes are a single added group. The added lang keys are used by the new views, and the tests/Pest.php joinEntity helper is used by the tests.

issues.explanation: The public property $targetMembershipId has no #[Validate] rule, which goes against Livewire policy rule 1; the action's filter_var/admin lookup does make it safe.

delete() and transfer() (and Members::assignRole/removeMember) do not call $this->authorize themselves and rely on the action's Gate check; this is safe, but it is inconsistent with save()/addMember(), which authorize twice.
The tests declare global helper functions named settings() and members(), which could collide with other test files or helpers later.
Every action writes an audit log line, but the task only asks for one on pick; this is harmless but goes beyond the request.

review.summary: The change implements the entity data model, including a database-enforced single owner through a stored generated column, the policies, entity picking, and the dashboard, members and owner-only settings Livewire pages. Domain writes go through Actions with server-side authorization, untrusted ids are resolved safely, the entity is locked, and the tests cover unauthorized and tamper cases thoroughly. Only minor convention nits remain (an unvalidated public property that the action checks anyway), so I would approve it with nits.
